Foundations: Outcomes, Goals and Your Working Baseline

Productivity at work is about finishing the work that moves results, not about looking busy. In this module you learn the difference between output and activity, write work goals with SMART and OKRs, and measure how your working hours and attention are really spent today.

Ask ten people at a Lagos office or a market stall how their week went and many will say "very busy". Busy describes **activity**: messages answered, calls taken, meetings attended. Productivity describes **output**: the results your job or business exists to deliver. A customer service officer's output might be complaints resolved. A caterer's output is orders delivered on time and paid for. A head teacher's output includes lessons taught well and parents kept informed. This course is about growing output without adding hours.

When you know your results areas, you can judge any request by one question: does this move one of my results?

Deep work and shallow work

The writer and computer science professor **Cal Newport** popularised two useful labels in his book *Deep Work* (2016). **Deep work** is focused, demanding work that needs your full attention and creates real value: writing a proposal, designing a new product, preparing a budget, planning a training. **Shallow work** is easier, often logistical work that you can do while distracted: forwarding a file, confirming a meeting time, updating a register. Both are needed. The problem is that shallow work arrives all day by itself, while deep work only happens if you protect time for it.

A practical test: if a smart new colleague could do the task well after one week of training, it is probably shallow. If it needs your experience, judgement or creativity, it is probably deep. Most people find their key results depend on deep work, yet their days are filled with shallow work.
Why meetings cut a day into pieces

In a well known 2009 essay, the programmer and investor **Paul Graham** described the "maker's schedule" and the "manager's schedule". A manager's day is divided into hour slots, and a meeting simply fills one slot. A maker, someone who writes, designs, plans or builds, needs long unbroken stretches. One meeting at 11 a.m. can spoil a whole morning for a maker, because the time before it is too short to start something serious. Many women in work and business are both makers and managers, so the skill is to group meetings and calls together and keep separate blocks for making.

A goal turns your results areas into a target with a finish line. Without one, every week feels the same and it is hard to say no to anything. Two methods are widely used in workplaces around the world: **SMART goals** for clear individual targets, and **OKRs** (Objectives and Key Results) for ambitious targets that a person, team or business works towards over a quarter.

SMART goals

The SMART idea was published by **George T. Doran** in the journal *Management Review* in 1981. Today the letters are usually read as: **Specific** (what exactly), **Measurable** (a number or clear sign of completion), **Achievable** (possible with your time and resources), **Relevant** (linked to a results area) and **Time-bound** (a deadline).

OKRs: an objective plus key results

OKRs grew out of the management practice of **Andy Grove** at Intel. **John Doerr**, who learned the method at Intel, introduced it to Google in its early years and later wrote the book *Measure What Matters* (2018). An OKR has two parts:
**Objective**: what you want to achieve, written in plain, inspiring words. It has no number. For example: "Make our bakery the first choice for office events in Wuse."

**Key results**: usually three to five measurable signs that show you reached the objective. Each has a number and a date. For example: "Deliver 20 office orders this quarter", "Get 10 written reviews from office clients", "Repeat orders from at least 5 offices".
**Initiatives**: the actions you take to move the key results, such as building a price list for corporate packs. These are tasks, not key results.

A key result describes an outcome, not an activity. "Send 50 flyers" is an activity; "Get 10 new office enquiries" is a result. At Google, OKRs are often deliberately ambitious and scored from 0 to 1 at the end of the quarter, so reaching most but not all of a stretch key result can still be a good outcome. If you use OKRs with a manager, agree in advance whether a key result is a firm commitment or a stretch target.

Which one should you use?

Use a **SMART goal** when the target is personal, clear and must be fully achieved, such as a report deadline or a sales quota set by your employer. Use an **OKR** when you want to stretch, when several people are involved, or when you need a few measures to describe one bigger aim. You can combine them: each key result should itself be specific, measurable and time-bound.
Worked example: a quarterly OKR for a fashion business
For example, Halima designs and sells women's clothing in Kano through Instagram and WhatsApp. Sales have been uneven. It is the start of the July to September quarter.
Objective: "Build steady monthly sales from returning customers."
Key result 1: 40 repeat customers by 30 September (she had about 15 in the last quarter, from her sales book).
Key result 2: Average order value of 25,000 naira (approximate) or more, up from about 18,000 naira.
Key result 3: 4 new collections announced on schedule, one every three weeks.
Initiatives: start a broadcast list of past buyers, create a matching scarf and bag add-on, plan the collection calendar.
Weekly action for week 1: tidy her contact list and label every past buyer, 1 hour on Monday and Thursday.
Halima can check her progress every Friday against three numbers instead of a general hope for "more sales". At the end of September she scores each key result and sets the next quarter's OKR.
Common mistakes when writing goals
**Too many key results**: ten measures for one objective means none gets attention. Keep three to five.
**Measuring effort instead of result**: "work harder on marketing" cannot be checked. Ask: what number would change if this worked?
**No baseline**: "increase repeat customers" means little if you do not know how many you have now. Look in your sales book or records first.
**Set and forget**: a goal written in January and read again in December has not guided anything. Check key results weekly.
Keep it to a few
One to three objectives per quarter is plenty for one person. More than that and the goals compete for the same hours, which brings back the busy-but-stuck feeling the goals were meant to fix.

Before you change how you work, you need a starting measurement, called a **baseline**. Without it, you cannot tell later whether a new method helped. This lesson uses a short work log focused on three things: what you worked on, how long you stayed focused, and what pulled you away. Classify your interruptions
An interruption is anything that stops the task you chose and makes you switch to another. Give each one a source code so patterns appear:
**W**: WhatsApp or SMS message you opened
**E**: email notification you checked
**C**: phone call
**P**: a person at your desk or shop counter
**S**: self-interruption, such as picking up the phone "just to check" or jumping to an easier task

Self-interruptions surprise many people. If most of your tally marks are S, the fix is about habits and phone settings. If most are P, it is about agreements with colleagues or customers. If most are W or E, Module 2 Lesson 3 will help directly.
Calculate your numbers
**Focused deep-work hours**: add up only the blocks marked Deep that had zero or one interruption. Divide by three for a daily average.
**Interruptions per day**: add all tally marks and divide by three.
**Time on results**: add the hours linked to a results area, divide by total working hours and turn it into a percentage.
**Fixed commitments**: total the hours in meetings, set duties (such as opening the shop or school runs during work hours) and travel.
**Planned capacity**: working hours minus fixed commitments minus a buffer of about 20 percent for the unexpected. This is how much you can realistically plan into a day.

Worked example: an office baseline
For example, Funke is a programme officer at an NGO in Ibadan. She works 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., 8 hours a day, and feels she never has time to write donor reports.
Over three days she logs 24 hours. Blocks marked Deep with zero or one interruption total 3 hours, so her daily average is 1 hour of focused deep work.
She tallies 69 interruptions in three days, an average of 23 per day: W 31, P 18, S 14, C 6.
Hours linked to a results area total 13 out of 24, so 54 percent of her time is on results.
Fixed commitments: 2 hours of meetings a day on average. Capacity: 8 minus 2 is 6 hours; minus a 20 percent buffer (about 1.2 hours) leaves about 4.8 hours she can plan.
Her biggest drain, with evidence: WhatsApp (31 interruptions), mostly from a staff group chat that is busy all day.
Funke's baseline is: 1 focused hour a day, 23 interruptions a day, 54 percent of time on results, about 4.8 plannable hours. Her first target is the staff group chat.
Do not plan to 100 percent

If your plan fills every working hour, the first urgent request breaks the whole day. Planning to your real capacity, with a buffer, is what makes a plan believable. Many people find their daily to-do list has two or three times more work than their capacity allows.
Reading your results honestly

Look at your numbers before deciding what to change. Low deep-work hours with many W or E marks point to message habits. Low deep-work hours with few interruptions but many meetings point to a calendar problem. A low percentage of time on results with few interruptions often means unclear priorities: you are working steadily, but on the wrong things. Pick the one pattern that costs you most. Trying to fix everything at once usually means nothing changes.
Privacy at work
If you log in an office, keep client names and confidential details out of the log. Write "Client A report" rather than the client's name, especially if you use a shared device.

Many people keep their work in their heads, on scraps of paper, in WhatsApp chats starred "for later" and in half-remembered promises made in meetings. The result is a constant feeling of something forgotten. **David Allen**, author of *Getting Things Done* (first published in 2001), argues that the mind is for having ideas, not holding them. His method, usually called **GTD**, gives every commitment a home outside your head so you can focus on one thing at a time.
A person adding items to a large task list
Every work commitment goes into one trusted list, not into your memory.
The five steps of GTD
The GTD workflow
Capture
Clarify
Organise
Reflect

Collect everything, decide what each item means, put it in the right list, review it weekly, then do the work.
**Capture**: collect anything that has your attention (requests, ideas, promises) into an inbox. One inbox is best.

**Clarify**: for each item ask "Is it actionable?" If not, delete it, file it for reference or put it on a someday list. If yes, decide the very next physical action. If that action takes less than two minutes, do it now.

**Organise**: put actions where they belong: a next-actions list, a calendar (for things fixed to a date and time), a waiting-for list (things others owe you) or a projects list (outcomes needing more than one step).
**Reflect**: review the lists regularly, especially in a weekly review (Module 3, Lesson 3).
**Engage**: choose what to do now based on where you are, the time and energy you have, and your priorities.
Next actions: the key skill

Items such as "staff welfare" or "Lagos client" sit on lists for weeks because they are not actions. A **next action** starts with a verb and is something you could do right away: "Call Mrs Bello to confirm the venue", "Draft three questions for the staff welfare survey", "Email the Lagos client the revised quote". A **project** is any outcome that needs more than one action, such as "End-of-year staff party held". Keep the project on a projects list and always have at least one next action for it.

Both apps are free with a Google account, work on Android and iPhone, and sync with a computer. **Google Tasks** is best for actions: each task can have a due date, a time, notes, subtasks and a repeat setting, and tasks with dates show in Google Calendar. You can also open Tasks from the side panel in Gmail and turn an email into a task. **Google Keep** is best for capture and reference: quick notes, checklists, voice notes, photos of documents, labels and reminders.

A task list says **what** to do. A calendar says **when**. Time blocking joins the two: you give each important task a specific slot in your calendar, like an appointment with yourself. Cal Newport recommends planning every minute of the workday in blocks, then re-planning when things change. You do not need to be that strict. Blocking even your top two or three tasks makes a large difference, because a task with a time is much more likely to happen than a task on a list.
A person arranging blocks on a digital calendar
Time blocking turns your task list into appointments with yourself.
How to block a day
Check your planned capacity from Module 1, Lesson 3 (for example, about 5 hours).
Put fixed meetings and duties into Google Calendar first.
Choose your most important task and block 60 to 120 minutes for it in your best-energy hours. Name the block with the action, such as "Write board report section 2", not just "Work".
Add one or two blocks for batched shallow work, such as "Messages and email" at 11:30 a.m. and 3:30 p.m.
Leave a buffer block in the afternoon for things that come up.
Use a different colour for deep work, shallow batches and meetings so you can see the balance at a glance.

Useful Google Calendar features: you can make a block **repeat** every weekday; set notifications 5 minutes before a block starts; and on many work or school Google accounts you can create a **Focus time** event, which can automatically decline meeting invitations during that block. If you have a personal Gmail account, an ordinary event named "Focus: proposal" and marked Busy works as a visible signal to anyone who can see your calendar.
Pomodoro: focus in short sprints

The **Pomodoro Technique** was developed by **Francesco Cirillo** in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer. The basic cycle: choose one task, work on it for 25 minutes without switching, take a short break of about 5 minutes, and after four of these sessions take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. Pomodoro works well inside a time block: a 2-hour deep-work block holds about four sessions. If a thought or request interrupts you, write it in your capture inbox and return to the task.

Batching: group similar tasks

Each time you switch between different kinds of task, you lose time getting back into the first one. **Batching** means doing similar tasks together in one block: all calls, all payments and transfers, all invoices, all social media posts. For a small business, a weekly batch might be "Monday 4 p.m.: pay suppliers and record transfers on Moniepoint or Opay" rather than paying one supplier at a time throughout the week.
Worked example: blocking a sales manager's Wednesday

For example, Chioma is a sales manager at a distribution company in Abuja. Her capacity is about 5 hours. On Wednesday she must prepare a monthly sales review, approve 12 expense claims and handle customer calls.
Fixed items: team meeting 1:00 to 2:00 p.m. and a client visit 2:30 to 3:30 p.m. go into Google Calendar first.
Deep block: 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. "Prepare monthly sales review", run as four 25-minute Pomodoros with 5-minute breaks.
Batch 1: 11:15 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. "Calls and messages". She tells her team she will return calls in that slot.
Batch 2: 3:45 to 4:30 p.m. "Approve expense claims": all 12 at once, about 3 to 4 minutes each.
Buffer: 4:30 to 5:00 p.m. for anything that came up, then a 5-minute shutdown to plan Thursday.
Chioma finishes the sales review by 11 a.m. instead of late at night, approves all claims in one sitting and still handles every call, just in a planned slot.
Protecting the block
Before the block starts, open only the file or materials you need and close other tabs.
Put the phone face down or out of reach, with notifications paused (Lesson 3 shows how).
If you share an office or shop, tell colleagues the time you will be free, for example "I am finishing the report until 11, I will come to you then".
Start on time. A block that begins 20 minutes late is a smaller block.
When the plan breaks

It will. A power cut, an urgent client or a sick child can wreck a morning. Do not abandon the method. Take two minutes to re-block the rest of the day: move the deep task to the next free block and drop or postpone the lowest-value item. A re-planned day is still a planned day.

For many workers in Nigeria, WhatsApp is where work happens: staff groups, client chats, supplier updates and payment confirmations, all mixed with family and church groups. Email adds another stream. Each notification invites you to switch tasks. The goal of this lesson is not to ignore people, but to **decide when** you deal with messages, so that your best hours go to your most important work.
A person sorting and clearing items from an inbox
You decide when to process messages, so they stop deciding your day.
The four Ds for every message
When you open your inbox in a batch, make one decision per message, then move on. Do not read a message, close it and leave it for later without deciding.
The four Ds of message processing
Delete or archive it
Do it (under two minutes)
Delegate it to the right person
Defer it to a task or snooze
Every message leaves the inbox with one of four decisions, so nothing sits unread and undecided.
Gmail tools that save time

**Filters**: in Gmail on a computer, use the search bar options to create a filter, for example all emails from a supplier's address get a label "Suppliers" and skip the inbox, or newsletters are marked as read and archived.
**Labels**: like folders, but one email can have several. Keep them few, such as Clients, Suppliers, Finance, Reference.
**Snooze**: hides an email until a date and time you choose, then returns it to the top of your inbox. Use it for messages you cannot act on yet.
**Schedule send**: write a reply now and choose when it is delivered, for example 8 a.m. tomorrow, so you do not train people to expect replies late at night.
**Templates**: save replies you send often (turn them on in Gmail settings under Advanced), such as your price list response or meeting confirmation.
**Add to Tasks**: from the Gmail side panel, turn an email into a Google Task so it joins your task system.
WhatsApp tools that save time
**Mute**: mute busy groups for 8 hours, 1 week or always. Muted chats still receive messages; you just are not interrupted.
**Archive**: move chats out of the main list. With the "keep chats archived" setting on, they stay archived when new messages arrive.
**Pin**: pin your most important work chats to the top so they are easy to check during a batch.
**Notifications**: turn off message previews and group notifications in WhatsApp settings if you want quiet focus time.

**WhatsApp Business** (free app for businesses): **quick replies** for frequent answers (typed with a shortcut beginning with "/"), an **away message** outside business hours, a **greeting message** for new customers, **labels** such as "New order" or "Paid", and a **catalogue** so customers can see products without asking you each time.

Your phone helps too. On Android, **Digital Wellbeing** has a Focus mode that pauses chosen apps; on iPhone, **Focus** lets you choose which people and apps can notify you, so calls from your manager or your children's school still come through while group chats wait.
Worked example: a caterer takes back her mornings
For example, Bukola runs a catering business in Lagos. Her baseline showed 28 WhatsApp interruptions a day and only 30 minutes of focused menu planning and costing.
She moves customer chats to WhatsApp Business and creates 5 quick replies: price list, delivery areas, how to pay, order deadline and menu for the week.
She labels chats "New enquiry", "Order confirmed" and "Paid", so she can see where each customer is without scrolling.
She mutes 6 non-urgent groups for "always" and checks them once a day at 4 p.m.

She sets three message batches: 8:00, 12:30 and 4:00 p.m., about 30 minutes each, and adds a line to her WhatsApp Business profile: "Messages answered at 8am, 12:30pm and 4pm. For same-day emergencies, please call."
During her 9:00 to 11:00 a.m. focus block she switches on Focus mode, allowing calls only.

After two weeks her interruptions fall to about 6 a day (mostly calls), she gets close to 2 focused hours each morning, and customers still receive answers within a few hours. Quick replies cut her typing in each batch.
Agree response times

Batching works best when people know what to expect. Agree a simple rule with your manager and team, such as "WhatsApp messages answered within 3 working hours; anything truly urgent, please call". For customers, state your hours and response times on your WhatsApp Business profile and in your away message. Clear expectations remove the pressure to reply instantly, and they make you look more organised, not less available.
Watch for message scams

Batching messages also gives you time to check them calmly. Be suspicious of urgent payment requests, new account numbers sent by "suppliers", or messages claiming to be from your bank. Confirm by calling a number you already know, and never share OTPs or PINs on WhatsApp.

A good system must work week after week without wearing you out. This module covers delegating work clearly, recognising and preventing burnout at work, and running a weekly review with a few simple numbers that show whether your methods are really working.
Delegating work clearly and following up
Decide which tasks to delegate and which to keep
Write a clear delegation brief covering outcome, deadline, resources and authority
Choose a suitable level of authority for the person and task
Follow up using check-ins and a waiting-for list without micromanaging

If you are a supervisor, a business owner with even one assistant, or a team member who shares work with colleagues, you cannot do everything yourself. **Delegation** means handing a task to someone else while you stay responsible for the result. Done well, it frees your time for deep work on your key results and helps others grow. Done badly, it produces wrong work, rework and frustration, and many people then decide "it is faster to do it myself".
Two people discussing a written task brief
A clear brief is the difference between delegation that works and rework.
What to delegate

Go through your Next actions list and your Module 1 log. Good candidates to delegate are tasks that are repeated often, that someone else can learn, or that someone else can do well enough at lower cost. Tasks to keep are those only you can do: decisions that need your authority, sensitive conversations, and the deep work tied to your key results.
Delegate (for example)
Keep (for example)

Write a delegation brief
Most failed delegation is a briefing problem. Give the brief in writing (a short WhatsApp message, email or Google Doc) even if you also explain it in person. Cover five points:
**Outcome**: what "done" looks like. "A list of all items below reorder level, with quantities and supplier, in the shared sheet" is clearer than "check the stock".
**Deadline**: a date and time, plus any check-in point.
**Resources**: files, money, contacts, templates or examples of good past work.
**Authority**: what they can decide alone and what needs your approval, such as "you can spend up to 20,000 naira without asking me".
**Check-in**: when and how you will review progress.
Match authority to experience

A new staff member may need a clear method and approval before acting. An experienced colleague may only need the outcome and deadline. A useful way to think about it is a ladder of authority, from "Do exactly this" to "Decide and act, tell me afterwards". Choose the rung for each task and person, and say it out loud so there is no confusion.
Ladder of delegated authority
Decide, act, report later
Decide, act, tell me now
Recommend, I decide
Investigate and report back
Do exactly as instructed
Start lower for new people and new tasks, and move up the ladder as trust and skill grow.
Worked example: delegating weekly stock control
For example, Esther owns a provisions shop in Ilorin and spends about 3 hours every Saturday counting stock and preparing orders. Her shop assistant, Kunle, has worked with her for 8 months.

She writes a brief on WhatsApp: outcome (reorder list in a shared Google Sheet with item, quantity left, quantity to order, supplier), deadline (Saturday 1 p.m.), resources (the sheet template and supplier price list), authority (Kunle prepares the list; Esther approves and pays).
Week 1: they count together and she shows how she decides reorder quantities. Authority level: do exactly as instructed.
Weeks 2 and 3: Kunle counts alone; Esther checks 10 items at random. Two errors in week 2, none in week 3.
Week 4: she moves him up to "recommend, I decide". Her time on stock falls to about 30 minutes of checking and approval.
She records the task on her Waiting-for list every Saturday until the habit is reliable.
Esther saves about 2.5 hours each week, which she uses for a new Saturday deep-work block: building relationships with two nearby schools for bulk orders.
Following up without micromanaging

Agree check-ins in advance so they feel normal, not like suspicion: for a one-week task, a short check halfway is usually enough. At the check-in, ask what is done, what is blocking progress and what help is needed. When the work comes back, give specific feedback: what was good, and one thing to change next time. Resist redoing the work yourself; instead, explain the gap and let the person fix it, so they learn and the task stays delegated.
Delegation is not dumping

Hand over the task with the training, tools and authority to do it, and give credit when it is done well. Delegating only unpleasant work with no support, or taking back tasks at the first mistake, destroys trust. Also never delegate access to your bank app, PINs or passwords; use separate staff logins or approval limits where your bank or payment app provides them.
Upward delegation
If a colleague keeps bringing problems back for you to solve, ask "What do you recommend?" before giving your answer. Over time this builds their judgement and keeps the task with them.
Delegate repeated, learnable tasks; keep decisions and key deep work.

Avoiding burnout: sustainable pace at work
Describe burnout using the World Health Organization's three dimensions
Recognise early warning signs in yourself and your team

Know when and where to seek help

A productivity system that pushes you to do more and more can make things worse. Productivity is meant to help you do the right work and then **stop**. In 2019 the **World Health Organization (WHO)** included burn-out in the 11th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) as an **occupational phenomenon**, not a medical condition. WHO describes it as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.
A person closing a laptop and leaving work at the end of the day
A clear end to the workday is part of a productive system, not a break from it.
The three dimensions
WHO describes burn-out with three dimensions. Knowing them helps you notice it early, in yourself or in a colleague.
How unmanaged work stress builds burnout
Overload and long hours
Exhaustion
Mental distance and cynicism
Reduced effectiveness
More hours to catch up
When the response to falling effectiveness is simply more hours, the cycle feeds itself; breaking it needs a change in workload or recovery.
**Exhaustion**: feelings of energy depletion. Rest at the weekend no longer restores you.
**Mental distance**: increased mental distance from your job, or feelings of negativism or cynicism about it. You stop caring about work that used to matter.
**Reduced professional efficacy**: you feel less effective and accomplish less, even when you work longer.
Early warning signs to watch
Regularly working late or at weekends just to keep up, not for a short, planned peak.
Answering work messages in bed or during family time because you fear falling behind.
Dreading Monday from Saturday evening.
Making more small mistakes and taking longer over simple tasks.
Skipping meals, breaks or exercise because there is "no time".
Practical protections

**1. A shutdown routine.** End the workday with 10 minutes to capture loose ends into your inbox, check tomorrow's calendar and choose the first task. Then stop. Cal Newport recommends a fixed ritual like this so that work stops occupying your mind in the evening. If you work from home, close the laptop or put the work phone away as a clear signal.

**2. Use your capacity number.** When a new request arrives and your week is already full to capacity, something must move. Ask your manager which task should give way rather than silently adding hours: "I can take on the audit preparation. To do it by Friday, I would move the training plan to next week. Which do you prefer?"

**3. Protect breaks and leave.** Short breaks between Pomodoros and a real lunch break restore attention. Plan annual leave early and set an out-of-office reply in Gmail (and an away message in WhatsApp Business) so you can actually rest.

**4. Look after the basics.** Sleep, regular meals, water and some movement during the day are not luxuries for a busy person; they are what attention runs on. A short walk between blocks or stretching during a Pomodoro break helps more than scrolling through your phone.

**5. If you lead a team, watch your team too.** Notice colleagues who are always online late, who have become withdrawn or who are making unusual mistakes. Ask privately how they are coping with their workload, and review how work is shared before pushing for more output.
Worked example: a workload conversation

For example, Adaeze is an accountant at a mid-sized company in Enugu. For six weeks she has worked until 9 p.m. most days. Her weekly review shows she completed only 2 of her 5 planned priorities last week, and she feels drained every morning.

She lists her current commitments with estimated hours: month-end close (14), payroll (6), audit preparation (10), supplier reconciliations (8), ad hoc requests (about 8). Total: 46 hours against a capacity of about 32 hours.
She identifies tasks that could move or be shared: supplier reconciliations could go to the junior accountant with a brief; audit preparation could start a week later.
She books 20 minutes with her manager and presents the list: "I have about 46 hours of work and 32 hours of real capacity. I suggest these two changes. Which would you prefer?"
They agree to delegate reconciliations and move one audit deadline. She sets a shutdown routine at 5:30 p.m. and a Focus block every morning.
Her planned work falls to about 34 hours. Within three weeks she is leaving by 6 p.m. on most days and completing 4 of 5 weekly priorities.
When to seek help

If exhaustion, low mood, poor sleep or loss of interest continue for weeks, or affect your health and relationships, speak to a doctor or a qualified counsellor, and to your HR department if your workplace has one. If you ever feel unable to cope or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a health professional or emergency services immediately and tell someone you trust.

Systems decay. Lists fill with old items, the calendar drifts back to reactive days, and quick replies go out of date. David Allen calls the **weekly review** the critical success factor of GTD, the step that keeps the whole system trusted. In this lesson you combine the weekly review with a short scorecard so that you have evidence, not just feelings, about whether your methods are working.

The weekly review in three parts
Choose a fixed slot, such as Friday at 3:30 p.m. or Monday at 8 a.m., and block it in Google Calendar as a repeating event. Allen groups the review into three parts:
**Get clear**: empty your capture inbox, Gmail starred items and WhatsApp saved messages. Clarify every item into your lists. Clear your desk and notebook pages.

**Get current**: go through Next actions (tick off finished items, delete dead ones), Waiting for (follow up on anything overdue), Projects (each one has a next action) and the last and next two weeks of your calendar.
**Get creative**: look at your someday list and your OKR. Is there a new idea, opportunity or risk to act on?

Do the review at your desk with your phone, notebook and computer in front of you, so you can empty every inbox in one sitting. Many people like Friday afternoon because the week is fresh in their mind and Monday starts with a ready plan.
Then plan the next week: choose your top three priorities, each linked to a key result, and block time for them in Google Calendar before the week fills up.

Reading the numbers
**Priorities often unfinished, focused hours fine**: you are probably planning more than your capacity. Choose smaller priorities or fewer.
**Focused hours low, interruptions high**: return to Module 2, Lesson 3 and tighten one message habit.
**Everything improving, key result flat**: you are being efficient on the wrong work. Check that your weekly priorities really drive the key result.
**Energy falling for two or more weeks**: reduce load before output falls (Lesson 2).
Worked example: four weeks of scorecards
For example, Funke (the programme officer from Module 1) started with a baseline of 1 focused hour a day, 23 interruptions a day and no clear weekly priorities.
Week 1: priorities 1 of 3, focused hours 6 for the week, interruptions 15, energy 3. Cause: she planned three large reports. Adjustment: break reports into sections.
Week 2: priorities 2 of 3, focused hours 8, interruptions 14, energy 3. Cause: the staff group chat still pulls her in. Adjustment: mute it and check at 12 and 4.
Week 3: priorities 3 of 3, focused hours 9, interruptions 8, energy 4. No major problem; she keeps the system.
Week 4: priorities 3 of 3, focused hours 10, interruptions 7, energy 4. Key result "donor reports submitted on time": 2 of 2 this month.
In four weeks Funke's focused time roughly doubled from her baseline of about 5 hours a week, interruptions fell by about two thirds and she has numbers to show her manager.
Common review mistakes
**Skipping it when busy**: busy weeks are when the review matters most, because that is when lists fall out of date. Shorten it to 20 minutes rather than skip it.
**Only reviewing the to-do list**: the calendar, the waiting-for list and the OKR are where many surprises hide.
**Changing everything at once**: if you change three habits together and your numbers improve, you will not know which one helped.
**Judging yourself harshly**: the scorecard is information, not a grade. A bad week tells you what to adjust.
Keep the review short

If your review takes more than an hour, your lists are too long or you are doing work during the review. Note those tasks and do them in the week. A 30-minute review done every week beats a perfect 2-hour review done once a month.

Your capstone asks for a **specific, implemented change tested over at least a week, with an honest before-and-after comparison**. This lesson shows how to make that test fair. You treat your working method like a small experiment: one change, measured the same way as your baseline, long enough to see past one good or bad day. Two weeks is better than one, because the first few days of any new habit are unusual.

Step 1: choose one change

Step 2: write a hypothesis

A hypothesis is a prediction you can check. Use this pattern: "If I [change], then [measure] will move from [baseline] to [target] within [time]." For example: "If I batch WhatsApp into three slots a day, my interruptions will fall from 23 to under 10 a day, and my focused hours will rise from 1 to 2 a day, within two weeks." Write it down before you start, so you cannot quietly change the target later.
Step 3: run and record
Set up everything the change needs on day 0 (calendar blocks, filters, quick replies, the delegation brief).
Tell the people affected, such as your manager, team or regular customers.
Track the same measures as your baseline. At minimum, tally interruptions on three sample days each week and record focused hours daily.
Keep a short daily note: what worked, what got in the way, anything unusual (a public holiday, a power outage, a sick day).
Do not add a second change in the middle. Write new ideas on your someday list for later.

Step 4: compare fairly

Put the baseline and the experiment side by side in a table. Use averages per day or per week, not your best day. Note anything unusual that may have affected the numbers, such as a quiet week after a public holiday or a busy end-of-month period. If the experiment weeks were not typical, say so; honesty here is what makes your evidence believable.
Worked example: testing meeting blocks

For example, Rukayat is a project coordinator at a construction firm in Abuja. Her baseline showed 6 meetings a day spread from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., 0.5 focused hours a day and 2 of 5 weekly priorities completed.
Hypothesis: "If I move internal meetings into 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. and block 9 to 11:30 a.m. for deep work, my focused hours will rise from 0.5 to at least 2 a day within two weeks."
Day 0: she sets a repeating Focus time block from 9 to 11:30 a.m. in Google Calendar and messages her team: "From Monday, please book meetings with me between 1 and 4 p.m."
Week 1: focused hours average 1.6 a day; two site meetings still land in the morning because a client could only meet then.
Week 2: she offers the client two afternoon slots; focused hours average 2.2 a day. Weekly priorities completed: 4 of 5.
Comparison: focused hours from 0.5 to an average of 1.9 over two weeks; priorities from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5. Unusual factor: week 1 included a site inspection.
Rukayat keeps the change and adjusts it: client meetings are allowed in the morning once a week. She has clear, honest numbers for her capstone.

Tips for presenting numbers
**Use simple comparisons**: "from 23 to 7 a day" is clearer than percentages alone. Give both if you like.
**Show the time frame**: say how long you measured, such as "two-week test against a three-day baseline".
**Round sensibly**: "nearly 2 hours" is fine when your log shows 1.9. Do not round in your own favour.
**Add one picture**: a simple bar chart in Google Sheets of before and after for your main measure helps a busy reader.
**Lead with the result**: put the headline number in the first line of your report or message.
Answering interview questions

When asked "How do you manage your time?" or "Tell me about a time you handled a heavy workload", use the **STAR** structure, a common format for interview answers: **Situation** (the context), **Task** (what you needed to achieve), **Action** (what you did, step by step) and **Result** (what changed, with numbers). Your experiment fits it exactly. Practise saying it in under two minutes.
Suggesting a team improvement

If your change worked, others may benefit. Propose it carefully: share your own results first, suggest a small trial (for example, a two-week team agreement that the staff group chat is for announcements only, with replies batched at 12 and 4), and agree how you will all judge it. A suggestion backed by your own numbers is far more persuasive than a general complaint about too many messages.

Use your appraisal too. Many organisations hold mid-year or annual reviews where you are asked what you achieved. Bring your one-page report and scorecard. Numbers about how you improved your own working method show initiative, and they give your manager something specific to write about you.
Keep it honest and confidential

Report your real numbers, including what did not improve. Do not include colleagues' names, client details or confidential figures in a report you share outside your organisation. Ask your manager before sharing work data publicly, for example in a LinkedIn post.
